Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
At 60, Daniel, a European American warehouse worker living with his long-term partner, came to treatment carrying a history that still felt lodged in his body more than three decades after his military deployment. He described one night in particular, when an operation went wrong and men he had trained beside were killed while he survived. What stayed with him was not a clean narrative but fragments: the glare of headlights on dust, shouted orders, the smell of fuel, and the sight of uniforms torn and darkened. Since then, he had come to believe that surviving when others did not made him somehow stained, as if there were something fundamentally wrong with him. He spoke in the language of a man who no longer knew who he was, saying that he did not recognize himself anymore and that the world had become dangerous in a way he could never quite brace against.

Those beliefs shaped what Daniel could and could not allow himself to do. He avoided going anywhere near the area where the event had happened, even decades later, and would not drive past the old base or the road that passed close to it. At work in the warehouse, he also avoided wearing anything that reminded him of the fatigues and heavy gear from that period; even certain work shirts, with their stiff fabric and muted colors, made him feel exposed and uneasy, so he kept to the same plain clothes he had worn for years. He tried not to think about what happened, because when the memory came, it did not feel like a recollection at all but like being pulled back into the same terror he had felt then. That fear made him more certain that the world was unsafe and that he had somehow failed the men who did not make it out, which in turn deepened his shame and sense that he no longer understood his own character.

Daniel's memory of the event had become painfully disorganized over time. He could say what happened, but he often found himself unable to find the words, stopping mid-sentence and shaking his head as if language itself had gone missing. When he did manage to remember, the guilt hit him hard; he would lower his eyes and say he should have done more, should have died with them, should have been the one to stay behind. The memory was not softened by years passing. It remained vivid enough to bring back the same terror, and that terror made it harder for him to organize the story at all, leaving him even more stuck with the sense that the event must have meant something terrible about him. He noticed that whenever he touched on the memory, the old guilt and fear flooded back together, and he would quickly turn away from it, certain he was safer not giving it words.

Over the years, Daniel's efforts to keep distance from these feelings became increasingly organizing features of his life. He would reroute his driving to avoid any area that resembled the old base, and he felt a rising panic if a conversation turned toward military service or if he caught himself remembering too much. In the warehouse, a glimpse of similar clothing on a veteran coworker or a pile of khaki work uniforms in the locker room could make him tense and leave the area. But the more he avoided reminders, the more alone he felt with the belief that he had survived when others had not for no good reason, and the more dangerous the world seemed in his mind. The less he could tolerate remembering, the less able he was to put the event into words, and that silence fed the sense that something was wrong with him at the core. His partner had noticed him becoming more distant and watchful, as if he was always bracing for something he could not name, and Daniel himself admitted that he had started to feel like a stranger to his own life.

He finally sought help after a recent workday when a delivery route unexpectedly took him close to the old military site. He felt his chest tighten, his mind flood with the same terror, and for the rest of the day he could barely function at the warehouse, needing to keep to himself and leave early. What brought him in was not only the intensity of that reaction, but the fear that he was running out of ways to keep it contained. He was most afraid that if he kept avoiding the places, thoughts, and clothes tied to the trauma, his life would shrink even further around the guilt and fear he already carried. He also hoped, tentatively, that if he could finally find words for what happened, he might discover that he was more than the man he had come to believe himself to be.
